hu-badacsony.name: Badacsony
hu-badacsony.grapes: Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát, Kéknyelű, Furmint, Rajnai rizling, Budai, Hárslevelű
hu-badacsony.summary: Badacsony is the district of the basalt 'witness hills' on the north-west shore of Lake Balaton: Badacsony itself (437 m), with its columnar basalt 'organ pipes', plus Szent György-hegy, Gulács, Tóti-hegy and Csobánc. Sixteen settlements share it. The lake reflects light and heat onto the slopes and the basalt and tuff soils give whites of real density and smoky minerality. Olaszrizling and Szürkebarát (Pinot Gris) dominate; Badacsony is also the last real home of Kéknyelű, an old variety with functionally female flowers that has to be interplanted with a pollinator such as Budai zöld, and which the Badacsony research station saved from near extinction.
hu-badacsony.terroir: Basalt caps, basalt tuff and Pannonian sand on steep south-facing slopes above the lake.
hu-badacsony.nerd_note: The poet Sándor Kisfaludy's 18th-century press house on Badacsony is now a restaurant; the 'Rózsakő' stone above it is the legendary meeting place of local lovers.

hu-balaton.name: Balaton
hu-balaton.grapes: Olaszrizling and a wide range of permitted varieties
hu-balaton.summary: Balaton is the regional umbrella PDO covering the six Balaton districts (about 155 settlements). Producers use it to blend across districts or for simpler wines; the more specific district and village names carry the prestige.

hu-balaton-felvidek.name: Balaton-felvidék
hu-balaton-felvidek.grapes: Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát, Cserszegi fűszeres, Rajnai rizling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
hu-balaton-felvidek.summary: The Balaton Uplands district stretches across the hills north and west of Lake Balaton, from Cserszegtomaj and Gyenesdiás near Keszthely to Sümeg and the Káli basin (23 settlements). It mixes volcanic, limestone and sandstone soils and makes mostly fresh dry whites: Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát, Rajnai rizling and the aromatic Cserszegi fűszeres, which was bred at nearby Keszthely and named after Cserszegtomaj.

hu-balatonboglar.name: Balatonboglár
hu-balatonboglar.grapes: Chardonnay, Olaszrizling, Irsai Olivér, Muscat Ottonel, Pinot Noir, Kékfrankos, Merlot, Cabernet
hu-balatonboglar.summary: Balatonboglár covers the south shore of Lake Balaton and its hinterland (42 settlements in Somogy county). The soils are loess and sand, flatter and warmer than the north shore, and the wines are fruit-forward: aromatic whites, rosé, approachable reds and a great deal of sparkling wine, since the Balatonboglár winery (now Törley-owned) is a major sparkling producer. Ikon, Garamvári and Kristinus are among the estates.

hu-balatonfured-csopak.name: Balatonfüred-Csopak
hu-balatonfured-csopak.grapes: Olaszrizling, Rajnai rizling, Furmint, Chardonnay, Szürkebarát, Merlot, Cabernet
hu-balatonfured-csopak.summary: This district lines the north-east shore of Lake Balaton from Balatonalmádi through Csopak and Balatonfüred to Zánka, 27 settlements in all, including the Tihany peninsula. Its signature is the red Permian sandstone and slate that colours the soil around Csopak, Paloznak and Lovas, which gives taut, salty Olaszrizling. Balatonfüred, the spa town where Hungary's first Anna Ball was held, adds limestone and marl. In recent years the growers have split off narrower PDOs (Csopak in 2020, Füred in 2025) to promote stricter, terroir-based wines.

hu-bukk.name: Bükk
hu-bukk.grapes: Olaszrizling, Leányka, Királyleányka, Chardonnay, Kékfrankos, Zweigelt
hu-bukk.summary: Bükk is a small, cool district on the south-east slopes of the Bükk mountains near Miskolc, with 24 settlements including Bogács and Tibolddaróc, whose cellar villages are carved into rhyolite tuff. Olaszrizling, Leányka and Királyleányka make crisp whites; reds are light.

hu-csongrad.name: Csongrád
hu-csongrad.summary: Csongrád lies east of the Kunság on the sandy plains near Szeged and Csongrád along the Tisza (19 settlements). It is one of the warmest and driest parts of Hungary, producing mostly Kadarka, Kékfrankos and simple whites; its Kadarka has a small revival following.

hu-csopak.name: Csopak
hu-csopak.summary: Csopak is a narrow PDO (2020) covering five villages on the north-east shore of Balaton (Csopak, Alsóörs, Felsőörs, Lovas, Paloznak) and only two grapes, Olaszrizling and Furmint, with a maximum of 9 t/ha. It grew out of the 'Csopak Codex', a voluntary charter signed by local growers in 2012 to raise Olaszrizling to a terroir wine. The red Permian sandstone and slate soils give firm, saline, almond-scented whites that age well, and producers such as Jásdi and Szent Donát label them by named vineyards.
hu-csopak.nerd_note: Csopak's red earth is Permian sandstone, about 270 million years old, the same 'red bed' rock that colours the nearby village of Alsóörs.

hu-debroi-harslevelu.name: Debrői Hárslevelű
hu-debroi-harslevelu.summary: Debrő, at the eastern foot of the Mátra around Aldebrő, Feldebrő and Verpelét, has been known for Hárslevelű for centuries, and the village name is fused with the grape in this PDO (2007). The wines are soft, perfumed and honeyed, often with a touch of sweetness. The Feldebrő church crypt, with 11th-century frescoes, is one of the oldest in Hungary.

hu-duna.name: Duna
hu-duna.summary: Duna is the umbrella PDO for the three Great Plain districts (Kunság, Csongrád, Hajós-Baja), about 150 settlements, for cross-district wines. It is mostly used for fresh, inexpensive whites, rosé and light reds from the sandy plains, often sold in bulk or under brand names.

hu-eger.name: Eger
hu-eger.grapes: Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Syrah; whites Leányka, Királyleányka, Olaszrizling, Hárslevelű, Furmint
hu-eger.summary:
Eger is the baroque town of castles, minarets and cellar valleys at the foot of the Bükk hills, and its wine district is Hungary's most famous red-wine name after Villány. Its emblem is Egri Bikavér ('Bull's Blood of Eger'), a blend of at least three (Classicus) or four (Superior) red varieties dominated by Kékfrankos, with Kadarka, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Syrah in support; no single grape may dominate too heavily. The name rests on the legend of the 1552 siege, when István Dobó's defenders supposedly frightened the Ottomans with red-stained beards. In Communist times Bikavér became a cheap export brand; today's good versions are spicy, medium-bodied, cherry-fruited and fresh rather than heavy.

Since 2010 Eger has built a white counterpart, Egri Csillag ('Star of Eger'), a blend led by aromatic varieties such as Leányka, Királyleányka, Olaszrizling, Hárslevelű and Furmint. Both blends follow a pyramid of Classicus, Superior and Grand Superior with stricter yields, mapped vineyards and longer ageing at the top. The district's 19 settlements include Eger, Andornaktálya, Demjén, Egerszalók, Felsőtárkány, Noszvaj and Ostoros; Pinot Noir from the Nagy-Eged hill is the region's other claim to fame.
hu-eger.terroir: Rhyolite tuff (soft enough to carve the Szépasszony-völgy cellars), andesite, clay and some limestone on south-facing foothills; cooler than southern Hungary, so later harvests and higher acidity.
hu-eger.nerd_note: Nagy-Eged hill above Eger reaches about 535 m with very steep south slopes; its Pinot Noir and Kékfrankos are among the most structured reds in northern Hungary.

hu-etyek-buda.name: Etyek-Buda
hu-etyek-buda.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Olaszrizling, Zöld veltelini, Királyleányka, Pinot Noir
hu-etyek-buda.summary: Etyek-Buda covers the limestone plateau west of Budapest (Etyek, Bicske, Velence) plus the Buda hills and the capital's Budafok district. Its product specification describes lime-rich brown forest soils on limestone, average temperatures of 9.5 to 10.5 °C and constant north-westerly winds: ideal for crisp whites and sparkling base wine. József Törley founded his champagne-method house at Budafok in 1882, and by the early 1910s the area made about two million bottles a year. Today Etyek is Budapest's weekend wine village, with Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Királyleányka from producers such as Etyeki Kúria, Haraszthy and Nyakas.

hu-etyeki-pezsgo.name: Etyeki pezsgő
hu-etyeki-pezsgo.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and other permitted varieties
hu-etyeki-pezsgo.summary: Etyeki pezsgő is a sparkling-wine PDO approved by the European Commission in November 2025 for bottle-aged sparkling wine from the Etyek area. The Commission's summary cites limestone bedrock, constant wind and cool, humid air, which give fresh, citrus-fruited wines with firm acidity, and notes that older bottles develop biscuit and bread-crust notes. It formalises Etyek's long role as the vineyard of Budapest's sparkling-wine houses.

hu-fured.name: Füred
hu-fured.summary: Füred is a new village-level PDO, listed in the EU register in November 2025, for wines from Balatonfüred and neighbouring communities on the north shore of Lake Balaton. The European Commission's summary describes dry, fresh wines of medium intensity with crisp acidity. Like Csopak before it, it sits inside the larger Balatonfüred-Csopak district and is meant to give the historic spa town's growers a tighter, more site-focused label.
hu-fured.nerd_note: Balatonfüred has held its Anna Ball every July since 1825, one of the oldest society balls in Hungary.

hu-hajos-baja.name: Hajós-Baja
hu-hajos-baja.grapes: Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Zweigelt, Olaszrizling
hu-hajos-baja.summary: Hajós-Baja is the southern Great Plain district on the left bank of the Danube (17 settlements), on loess-covered sand that is a little richer than the Kunság's. It is famous for the cellar village (*pincefalu*) of Hajós, more than 1,200 cellars and press houses built by Swabian settlers on their own streets outside the village. Reds lead: Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Zweigelt.

hu-izsaki-arany-sarfeher.name: Izsáki Arany Sárfehér
hu-izsaki-arany-sarfeher.summary: A single-variety PDO (2007) for Arany Sárfehér ('golden yellow-white'), a high-acid, neutral old grape grown on the sands around Izsák in the Kunság. Its sharp acidity made it a good base for sparkling wine, and that is still its main use. Ten settlements are covered.

hu-kali.name: Káli
hu-kali.grapes: Olaszrizling, Furmint, Kéknyelű, Juhfark, Szürkebarát, Kékfrankos and others
hu-kali.summary: The Káli basin is a small enclosed valley behind Badacsony, ringed by basalt hills and littered with sandstone 'stone seas' (*kőtenger*). Its PDO (2009) covers eight villages such as Köveskál, Kővágóörs, Szentbékkálla and Salföld and allows a long list of varieties. It has become a magnet for Budapest weekenders and small natural-leaning growers who make textured whites from Olaszrizling, Furmint and Kéknyelű.

hu-koszeg.name: Kőszeg
hu-koszeg.grapes: Cool-climate whites and Kékfrankos (details in the 2025 specification)
hu-koszeg.summary: Kőszeg, a small walled town under the Alps' last foothills on the Austrian border, gained its own wine PDO in July 2025; the European Commission called it one of the oldest wine areas in Hungary. Its most famous custom is the *Szőlőjövés Könyve* (Book of the Coming of the Grapes): every year since 1740, on St George's Day (24 April), the length of the young vine shoots has been drawn into a town ledger, a unique 280-year phenological record.
hu-koszeg.nerd_note: The Book of the Coming of the Grapes is one of the longest continuous records of vine budbreak in Europe, now used by climate researchers.

hu-kunsag.name: Kunság
hu-kunsag.grapes: Olaszrizling, Ezerjó, Kövidinka, Cserszegi fűszeres, Arany sárfehér, Kékfrankos, Kadarka
hu-kunsag.summary: Kunság is Hungary's largest wine district, more than 100 settlements on the sandy plain between the Danube and Tisza around Kecskemét, Kiskőrös and Cegléd. The vineyards were planted on loose sand from the 1880s precisely because phylloxera cannot live in it, and the sand still makes ungrafted vines possible. Most of the output is light, inexpensive wine and sparkling base, but a few producers make lively whites from Ezerjó, Kövidinka, Cserszegi fűszeres and Olaszrizling and fresh Kadarka and Kékfrankos.
hu-kunsag.nerd_note: The Miklóstelep demonstration vineyard near Kecskemét, planted on land the town gave the state in 1883, proved that vines could be grown phylloxera-free on sand.

hu-matra.name: Mátra
hu-matra.grapes: Olaszrizling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscat Ottonel, Tramini, Zöld veltelini, Kékfrankos, Pinot Noir
hu-matra.summary: Mátra is Hungary's second-largest hill district, on the southern foothills of the Mátra mountains (Hungary's highest, peaking at Kékes, 1,014 m) around Gyöngyös, Abasár, Gyöngyöspata and Domoszló (36 settlements). Andesite and andesite tuff give fresh, aromatic whites (Olaszrizling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscat, Tramini, Zöld veltelini), and the cool slopes are increasingly used for Kékfrankos and Pinot Noir. Historically it fed Budapest's taverns; now growers such as Nagygombos, Szőke Mátyás and Benedek are building individual reputations.

hu-monor.name: Monor
hu-monor.grapes: Ezerjó, Olaszrizling, Kövidinka, Kékfrankos, Kadarka and others
hu-monor.summary: Monor (2018) is a small PDO for four settlements south-east of Budapest (Monor, Monorierdő, Bénye, Gomba), centred on the Monor cellar hill (Strázsahegy), which holds about 900 small cellars, one of the largest cellar villages in Hungary.

hu-mor.name: Mór
hu-mor.grapes: Ezerjó, Tramini, Rajnai rizling, Chardonnay, Leányka
hu-mor.summary: Mór, between the Vértes and Bakony hills, is the smallest Northern Pannonian district (six settlements) and the home of Ezerjó, a sharp, lean white once made both dry and as a botrytised sweet wine. Swabian settlers rebuilt the vineyards after the Ottoman wars; the 1956 'Ezerjó' tradition and a few dedicated growers keep the grape alive today.

hu-nagy-somlo.name: Nagy-Somló
hu-nagy-somlo.grapes: Olaszrizling, Furmint, Hárslevelű, Chardonnay, Rajnai rizling, Szürkebarát and others
hu-nagy-somlo.summary: Nagy-Somló ('Greater Somló') is the broader district PDO around Somló hill, adding five settlements to the five of Somló proper, including Celldömölk at the foot of the Ság hill and Kissomlyó. It permits a wider range of white varieties (Chardonnay, Rajnai rizling, Szürkebarát, Cserszegi fűszeres and others) and higher yields than the strict Somlói PDO, and it is used mainly for simpler whites from the volcanic satellites of the main hill.

hu-neszmely.name: Neszmély
hu-neszmely.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Irsai Olivér, Chardonnay, Olaszrizling, Cserszegi fűszeres
hu-neszmely.summary: Neszmély runs along the south bank of the Danube between Komárom and Esztergom (27 settlements). It is a cool, breezy white-wine district best known for the large modern Hilltop Neszmély winery, which pioneered clean, fruit-driven Hungarian whites for export in the 1990s. Sauvignon Blanc, Irsai Olivér, Chardonnay and Cserszegi fűszeres lead.

hu-pannon.name: Pannon
hu-pannon.summary: Pannon is the umbrella PDO for the four southern Transdanubian districts (Villány, Szekszárd, Pécs and Tolna), about 120 settlements, used for cross-district blends and simpler wines. It lets a producer blend Szekszárd Kékfrankos with Villány Cabernet, for instance, and still sell a protected-origin wine; the district names carry the prestige.

hu-pannonhalma.name: Pannonhalma
hu-pannonhalma.grapes: Rajnai rizling, Olaszrizling, Sauvignon Blanc, Tramini, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir
hu-pannonhalma.summary: Pannonhalma is the district below the Benedictine Archabbey of Pannonhalma, founded in 996 and a UNESCO site. The monks have made wine here for over a thousand years; the abbey's modern winery, rebuilt in 2003, makes precise whites (Rajnai rizling, Sauvignon Blanc, Tramini, Olaszrizling) and Pinot Noir from cool, windy slopes. Sixteen settlements around Győr belong to the district.

hu-pecs.name: Pécs
hu-pecs.grapes: Cirfandli, Olaszrizling, Chardonnay, Kékfrankos, Cabernet, Merlot
hu-pecs.summary: Pécs spreads over the warm southern slopes of the Mecsek hills around the city of Pécs, Roman Sopianae, and south to Mohács (33 settlements). It is the home of Cirfandli (Zierfandler), a spicy, late-ripening white that the local growers have taken as their emblem, and of the 19th-century Littke sparkling wine house.

hu-soltvadkerti.name: Soltvadkerti
hu-soltvadkerti.summary: Soltvadkerti (2020) is a one-commune PDO for Ezerjó from Soltvadkert on the Kunság sands, a town that once had one of the densest concentrations of vineyards on the Great Plain. The rules allow only Ezerjó, making a crisp, citrusy white.

hu-somloi.name: Somlói
hu-somloi.summary:
Somló is a single extinct volcano, a basalt butte rising 432 m out of the flat Kisalföld, and the smallest of Hungary's districts (about 300 to 400 ha in five settlements: Somlóvásárhely, Somlójenő, Somlószőlős, Doba and Borszörcsök). Its wines are among the most distinctive whites in Europe: dense, smoky, saline and austere in youth, built for years in bottle. The PDO allows only white grapes, led by Juhfark ('sheep's tail', after its long cylindrical bunches), Olaszrizling, Furmint, Hárslevelű and Tramini.

Somló's legend is that its wine guarantees a male heir. The Habsburg court is said to have served it on wedding nights, and the 'wedding night wine' story is still told at every cellar door. In the 19th century the Benedictine and Ursuline orders and noble families owned plots, and their small stone press houses still dot the slopes beneath the ruined castle. Today the hill is split among dozens of tiny growers; Kreinbacher's traditional-method sparkling wines are the most visible modern success.
hu-somloi.terroir: Basalt cap and basalt tuff over Pannonian sand and clay; steep south and south-west slopes around a solitary hill that catches heat and wind on a flat plain.
hu-somloi.nerd_note: Béla Fekete's Juhfark and Hárslevelű, aged in large old casks and released with years of age, showed how slowly the hill's wines evolve.

hu-sopron.name: Sopron
hu-sopron.grapes: Kékfrankos, Zweigelt, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir; Zöld veltelini, Tramini, Sauvignon Blanc
hu-sopron.summary: Sopron, hugging the Austrian border on the south-west shore of Lake Fertő (Neusiedlersee), is Hungary's Kékfrankos country: about 60 percent of its vineyards are planted to it. It is the Hungarian continuation of Burgenland, and its wines (crunchy, spicy, sour-cherry reds) resemble those across the border. The town's Swabian growers (*poncichter*, from the German 'Bohnenzüchter', bean-growers, for the beans they grew between vine rows) kept the tradition alive. Franz Weninger's biodynamic estate at Balf and Ráspi in Fertőrákos are leading names; the district covers 18 settlements, extending south to Kőszeg's hills.
hu-sopron.nerd_note: The Fertőrákos limestone quarry, worked since Roman times, is part of the Fertő/Neusiedlersee UNESCO landscape; the same Leitha limestone underlies some of Sopron's best Kékfrankos.

hu-szekszard.name: Szekszárd
hu-szekszard.grapes: Kadarka, Kékfrankos, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir; Olaszrizling, Chardonnay
hu-szekszard.summary:
Szekszárd sits on a block of deep loess hills above the Danube floodplain, about 150 km south of Budapest, with 15 settlements around the county town. The loess, in places tens of metres thick and cut into sunken lanes, gives the country's silkiest, most fragrant reds. The district's heritage grape is Kadarka, brought by Serbian settlers after the Ottoman era, which once made Szekszárd famous across the Habsburg lands. Phylloxera and Communist-era replanting replaced most of it with Kékfrankos and Bordeaux varieties, but growers such as Heimann and Takler have revived old Kadarka clones.

Szekszárdi Bikavér, a blend with a minimum share of Kadarka and led by Kékfrankos, is the district's answer to Eger and has strict local rules. Bordeaux blends, Merlot and Cabernet Franc can be excellent, and the loess makes softer, rounder versions than Villány's limestone. The district was home to the poet Mihály Babits and to some of Hungary's most respected family estates.
hu-szekszard.terroir: Thick Pleistocene loess over red clay (*vörösagyag*) and some limestone; deep sunken lanes (*löszmélyutak*); warm, sunny and fairly dry.
hu-szekszard.nerd_note: Heimann's Kadarka comes from a project that collected and replanted dozens of old Kadarka clones from local vineyards, rescuing the genetic diversity that commercial clones had lost.

hu-tihany.name: Tihany
hu-tihany.grapes: Kékfrankos, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Zweigelt, Portugieser
hu-tihany.summary: Tihany is a single-commune PDO on the volcanic peninsula that almost cuts Lake Balaton in two, crowned by the Benedictine abbey founded in 1055. Unusually for the north shore, the PDO is red-only: Kékfrankos, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Zweigelt and Portugieser, at no more than 55 hl/ha. The peninsula's geyser cones, basalt tuff and warm microclimate ripen red grapes reliably, and the abbey's 11th-century charter is among the first documents to mention vineyards in Hungary.
hu-tihany.nerd_note: The Tihany abbey's 1055 founding charter, written in Latin, contains the oldest surviving sentence fragment in Hungarian.

hu-tokaj.name: Tokaj
hu-tokaj.grapes: Furmint, Hárslevelű, Sárgamuskotály, Kövérszőlő, Zéta, Kabar
hu-tokaj.summary:
Tokaj is the one Hungarian appellation every wine lover knows, and one of the handful of sweet-wine regions in the world with genuine claim to greatness. It covers 27 settlements in the volcanic Zemplén foothills, from Abaújszántó and Monok in the west to Sátoraljaújhely in the north-east and Tokaj town at the confluence of the Bodrog and Tisza in the south. The official list in the current specification is: Abaújszántó, Bekecs, Bodrogkeresztúr, Bodrogkisfalud, Bodrogolaszi, Erdőbénye, Erdőhorváti, Golop, Hercegkút, Legyesbénye, Makkoshotyka, Mád, Mezőzombor, Monok, Olaszliszka, Rátka, Sárazsadány, Sárospatak, Sátoraljaújhely, Szegi, Szegilong, Szerencs, Tarcal, Tállya, Tokaj, Tolcsva and Vámosújfalu. (Ond, often listed separately, is now part of Szerencs.) Only vineyard land rated Class I or II in the cadastre counts.

What makes Tokaj special is the meeting of a late-ripening, high-acid grape (Furmint), a volcanic soil that gives the wine a smoky, saline grip, and a river microclimate that brings noble rot most autumns. The result is a family of wines unlike anything else: Eszencia, the near-unfermented nectar of aszú berries; Aszú, botrytised berries steeped in base wine, at least 120 g/l of sugar and 18 months in cask; Szamorodni, dry and nutty under flor or sweet; the rare Fordítás and Máslás; late harvest wines; and, since the 1990s, a fast-growing body of dry Furmint and Hárslevelű, often from named vineyards. Great Aszú tastes of apricot, orange peel, quince, honey, tea and walnut, with an acidity that keeps it fresh for a century.

The appellation is also one of the oldest legally protected wine regions in the world. Vineyards were ranked into classes between the 1720s and 1772, and a royal decree of 1737 limited the Tokaji name to defined towns and made new planting subject to permission. The landscape (cellars, villages, hills) has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2002.
hu-tokaj.terroir: Rhyolite, andesite and dacite with tuff layers, weathered to red *nyirok* clay or white kaolinitic soils; quartzite caps on some hills; loess on about 5% of the area (southern Tokaj hill around Tarcal and Tokaj). South-facing slopes of 120 to 300 m. Continental climate with long warm autumns; morning mists from the Bodrog and Tisza drive botrytis. Rock-cut cellars at 10 to 12 °C with walls furred in black cellar mould.
hu-tokaj.nerd_note: The modern 'puttonyos' label is only a hint: since 2013 every Aszú must have at least 120 g/l of sugar, '6 puttonyos' needs 150 g/l, and wines below 120 g/l can no longer be called Aszú at all. Old bottles labelled 3 or 4 puttonyos are pre-reform.

hu-tolna.name: Tolna
hu-tolna.grapes: Olaszrizling, Chardonnay, Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot
hu-tolna.summary: Tolna is a large, varied district between Szekszárd and Lake Balaton (54 settlements) with loess and sandy soils. It produces everyday whites, rosé and reds, and its Dunaföldvár and Bölcske corners on the Danube make some good Kékfrankos and Chardonnay.

hu-villany.name: Villány
hu-villany.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Portugieser, Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Pinot Noir; whites Olaszrizling, Hárslevelű, Chardonnay
hu-villany.summary:
Villány is Hungary's southernmost and warmest hill district, a 25 km strip along the southern face of the limestone Villány hills close to the Croatian border. Seventeen settlements belong to it, led by Villány, Villánykövesd, Palkonya, Nagyharsány and Siklós. After the Ottoman wars it was resettled by German 'Swabian' families, and their descendants (Bock, Gere, Tiffán, Polgár, Wunderlich, Heumann) built the cellar rows of Villány and Villánykövesd and led Hungary's first post-Communist quality revival. The district introduced Hungary's first origin-control system and the DHC (*Districtus Hungaricus Controllatus*) label term.

The wines are full-bodied, ripe reds. Portugieser (Kékoportó) was the old local grape for early-drinking wine; Bordeaux varieties took over after phylloxera and especially after 1990. Cabernet Franc proved the best fit, and in 2015 the growers created the Villányi Franc category, a premium Franc with strict yield, ageing and tasting rules. A quality pyramid of Classicus, Prémium and Villányi Franc, with single-vineyard wines from sites such as Kopár, Jammertal, Ördögárok and Konkoly, sits on top. Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Kékfrankos and Kadarka make up much of the rest, and Siklós, on the southern side, is known for whites.
hu-villany.terroir: Jurassic and Triassic limestone and dolomite under loess and red clay; sheltered south-facing slopes; sub-Mediterranean influence with hot summers and the highest sunshine hours in Hungary.
hu-villany.nerd_note: Zsigmond Teleki, born in Villány in 1854, established an experimental rootstock nursery there in 1881; his Berlandieri x Riparia seedlings were the source of rootstocks such as Kober 5BB and SO4, planted across Europe after phylloxera.

hu-zala.name: Zala
hu-zala.grapes: Olaszrizling, Tramini, Rajnai rizling, Zöld veltelini, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc
hu-zala.summary: Zala is the westernmost Balaton district, spread over the hills of Zala county towards the Slovenian and Croatian borders (37 settlements). It is wetter and cooler than the lake shore, with loamy, sometimes sandy soils, and makes light whites (Olaszrizling, Tramini, Rajnai rizling, Zöld veltelini) plus sparkling base wine.

sites.name: Tarcal
sites.text: Tarcal sits on the south-western foot of Tokaj hill, where loess drapes the volcanic core. It holds some of the region's most storied sites (Mézes Mály, Szarvas, Lónyai, Váti, Kassai), the Tokaj viticulture research station where Zéta and Kabar were bred, the Andrássy manor and Királyudvar's winery in a former royal court. Kikelet's loess Furmints showed how perfumed wines from this side of the hill can be.

sites.name: Tokaj
sites.text: The town that gave the region its name sits at the point of Tokaj hill (Kopasz-hegy, 514 m) where the Bodrog flows into the Tisza. River traffic once carried barrels north to Poland. The Rákóczi cellar under the main square, the Tokaj Museum and wineries such as Dobogó and Hétszőlő keep the town at the centre of the trade, and its southern slopes carry Hétszőlő and Szarvas.

sites.name: Mád
sites.text: Mád has the densest concentration of historic first-class vineyards in Tokaj: Szent Tamás, Úrágya, Betsek, Király, Nyulászó, Birsalmás, Percze and Danczka all surround the village, on rhyolite, andesite and quartzite. Royal Tokaji, Szepsy, Barta and Holdvölgy are based here, and the restored baroque synagogue recalls the Jewish merchants who ran much of the Tokaji trade until 1944.

sites.name: Tállya
sites.text: Tállya, a large market village on the western side of the hills, sits among andesite and rhyolite slopes with dűlők such as Hasznos and Dorgó. Its vineyards were among the Rákóczi family's holdings, and Lajos Kossuth, born in nearby Monok in 1802, was baptised in its Lutheran church. Its wines tend to be firm and spicy.

sites.name: Bodrogkeresztúr
sites.text: Bodrogkeresztúr lies on the Bodrog under the eastern face of Tokaj hill. The Lapis vineyard above it, a terraced rhyolite slope, is the source of Királyudvar's best wines, and the village has given its name to several fine Szamorodni. It is also a Hasidic pilgrimage site, home of the grave of the 'Kerestirer Rebbe', Reb Shayele Steiner.

sites.name: Erdőbénye
sites.text: A forested village in a side valley at the northern edge of the Tokaj hills, Erdőbénye was the region's cooperage centre, making the 136-litre Gönc casks and smaller barrels from local Zemplén oak. Máté Szepsi Laczkó served as pastor here; his memorial house stands on the main street. Béres and others work its cool, high dűlők such as Lőcse, Omlás and Határi.

sites.name: Olaszliszka
sites.text: Olaszliszka, on the Bodrog, carries in its name the 'olasz' (Latin, Italian) settlers invited after the Mongol invasion. Szepsi Laczkó Máté taught here before becoming a pastor. The Frenchman Samuel Tinon chose it for his winery, famous for long flor-aged dry Szamorodni, and Attila Homonna's work on the Határi slope helped put the village's cooler sites on the map.

sites.name: Sárospatak
sites.text: Sárospatak, on the Bodrog in the north-east, was the seat of the Rákóczi princes. Their castle, the Reformed College founded in 1531 (where Comenius taught), and the Rákóczi cellar beneath the town anchor its history. Today it hosts the Pajzos-Megyer winery, and the Megyer hill above Végardó is one of the north's historic vineyards.

sites.name: Sátoraljaújhely
sites.text: The northernmost Tokaj town sits on the Slovak border, facing Slovenské Nové Mesto, which belonged to it until 1920. On its castle hill lies the Oremus vineyard, source of the legendary 1631 aszú attributed to Szepsi Laczkó Máté and the name that the Vega Sicilia-owned estate took for its brand.

sites.name: Mezőzombor
sites.text: Mezőzombor, between Mád and Szerencs, is best known as home to Disznókő, the AXA-owned estate whose single block of about 150 ha takes in the Kapi and Dorgó sites. The village's lower, warmer slopes catch botrytis readily, which made it a reliable source of aszú berries.

sites.name: Rátka
sites.text: Rátka is a small village west of Mád, resettled by German-speaking Catholic families in the 18th century. Its main slope is the Padi-hegy, an andesite hill whose vineyards make firm, smoky Furmint.

sites.name: Szegi
sites.text: Szegi is a small Bodrog-side village between Bodrogkisfalud and Szegilong, with south-facing slopes such as Poklos. Its location on the river makes it a botrytis-friendly spot, and it has drawn several small modern growers.

sites.name: Szegilong
sites.text: Szegilong, on the right bank of the Bodrog north of Szegi, is one of the 27 settlements of the Tokaj PDO and one of the smallest. Its vineyards share the river mists that make the Bodrog side so reliable for noble rot.

sites.name: Bodrogkisfalud
sites.text: Bodrogkisfalud is a riverside village under Tokaj hill's north-eastern flank. The Patricius estate restored an 18th-century manor here, and the Csirke-mál slope above the village is a well-known site.

sites.name: Hercegkút
sites.text: Hercegkút ('Prince's Well') was settled by German Catholic families in the 18th century. Its two cellar rows, Kőporos and Gombos-hegy, with dozens of stone-fronted cellars dug into the hillside, are part of the core zone of the UNESCO Tokaj landscape.

sites.name: Makkoshotyka
sites.text: Makkoshotyka is a small upland village north-west of Sárospatak, at the forested edge of the Zemplén. It is one of the 27 Tokaj settlements, with few but cool vineyard slopes.

sites.name: Vámosújfalu
sites.text: Vámosújfalu ('customs new village') lies on the plain between Olaszliszka and Sárazsadány, its name recalling a medieval toll point. It is one of the quieter Tokaj settlements, with gentle slopes near the Bodrog.

sites.name: Tolcsva
sites.text: Tolcsva is one of Tokaj's great wine villages, with Oremus's winery and tunnel cellars, the headquarters of the state-owned Grand Tokaj (successor of the old state combine) and a wine museum. Sites such as Kincsem, Petrács and Kútpatka surround it, and noble rot was reportedly known here by 1527.

sites.name: Erdőhorváti
sites.text: Erdőhorváti is a forest village high in the Zemplén hills north of Tolcsva. Its few vineyards are among the coolest in the region, and the village is better known for its woods and walking routes than for wine.

sites.name: Bodrogolaszi
sites.text: Bodrogolaszi, another village named for its medieval Latin settlers, lies just south of Sárospatak. The Pajzos vineyard, one of the two historic estates of the Pajzos-Megyer winery, lies within its boundary.

sites.name: Golop
sites.text: Golop is a small village at the western margin of the region, between Tállya and Monok, on the edge of the Hernád valley. Its vineyards sit on the outer slopes of the Zemplén volcanic range.

sites.name: Monok
sites.text: Monok, at the far western rim of the Tokaj PDO, is famous as the birthplace of Lajos Kossuth (1802), leader of the 1848 revolution. Its vineyards face south over the Szerencs plain.

sites.name: Legyesbénye
sites.text: Legyesbénye is at the south-western end of the Tokaj crescent, near the Szerencs plain. It is a quiet village with gentle slopes, included among the 27 settlements of the PDO.

sites.name: Bekecs
sites.text: Bekecs, west of Szerencs, is one of the south-western edge villages of the region. Its gentle slopes give softer wines than the steep hills of Mád or Tarcal.

sites.name: Abaújszántó
sites.text: Abaújszántó marks the western end of Tokaj where the hills drop into the Hernád valley. Its Sátor-hegy ('Tent hill') and other volcanic slopes are farmed by the biodynamic Pendits estate, one of the region's early organic pioneers.

sites.name: Szerencs
sites.text: Szerencs is the gateway town at the south-western corner of Tokaj. The Rákóczi castle here hosted the 1605 diet that elected István Bocskai prince, and the town now includes Ond, whose Kőporos slope is a respected site. The town is also known for its chocolate factory.

sites.name: Sárazsadány
sites.text: Sárazsadány is a small village near the Bodrog between Vámosújfalu and Bodrogolaszi. It is one of the 27 Tokaj settlements, with gentle, botrytis-prone vineyards close to the river.

sites.name: Mézes Mály
sites.text: 'Honey pot' in old Hungarian, Mézes Mály in Tarcal was ranked a great first growth in the old classifications. About 19 ha of volcanic bedrock under deep loess on a warm south slope; Royal Tokaji owns about 11 ha and bottles both an Aszú and a dry Furmint from it. Its wines are rich and honeyed with a soft, broad texture from the loess.

sites.name: Szarvas
sites.text: Szarvas ('stag') lies on the southern foot of Tokaj hill between Tarcal and Tokaj and was rated a great first growth of the old classification. It was a royal and later Habsburg estate, and today belongs to the state-owned Grand Tokaj. Its loess and andesite give powerful, early-ripening aszú.

sites.name: Szent Tamás
sites.text: Named after St Thomas, this first-class Mád hillside of red nyirok clay and rhyolite tuff makes tense, smoky, saline wines. Szepsy's and the Szent Tamás winery's dry Furmints and Royal Tokaji's Aszú are its best-known bottlings.

sites.name: Úrágya
sites.text: Úrágya ('the lord's bed') lies on a high, steep slope north of Mád, on quartz-rich, silicified volcanic rock. Szepsy's and Királyudvar's dry Úrágya Furmint 2000 helped launch the dry single-vineyard movement, and the site still makes some of the most austere, long-lived dry wines in Tokaj.

sites.name: Betsek
sites.text: Betsek (also spelled Becsek) is a large first-class site east of Mád toward Bodrogkeresztúr, on rhyolite tuff and clay. Royal Tokaji's 1990 Betsek Aszú was among its first releases, and Dobogó and Szepsy also make wines from it.

sites.name: Király
sites.text: Király ('king') rises above Mád on rhyolite and red clay. Its steep upper part, Öreg Király ('old king'), was cleared and re-terraced by the Barta family from 2003 and is one of the steepest vineyards in the region; Szepsy also has parcels.

sites.name: Nyulászó
sites.text: Nyulászó ('hare-hunting place') is a first-class Mád site of volcanic clay that Royal Tokaji blends into its Aszú and bottles separately in good years. Its wines tend to be fine and spicy.

sites.name: Birsalmás
sites.text: Birsalmás ('quince orchard') lies on the western side of Mád. Royal Tokaji counts it among its first growths, and its name matches the quince note that classic Furmint often carries.

sites.name: Percze
sites.text: Percze is a small site close to the village of Mád, on rhyolite tuff; the Szepsy family consider it one of their best plots and named their Mád restaurant after it.

sites.name: Danczka
sites.text: Danczka (Dancka in the official list) sits around the Danczka-tető hilltop west of Mád. Its stony, windy slopes make tight, mineral dry wines, bottled by several of the Mád Circle growers.

sites.name: Bomboly
sites.text: Bomboly is a cool, elevated site north-east of Mád, with volcanic tuff soils. Its name appears on several modern single-vineyard dry Furmints. Being higher and more exposed, it ripens later than the village slopes and keeps notably bright acidity.

sites.name: Veresek
sites.text: Veresek ('the red ones') takes its name from the reddish volcanic clay of this Mád slope near the Bodrogkeresztúr border. It is a source of concentrated aszú berries.

sites.name: Hold-völgy
sites.text: Hold-völgy ('moon valley') is a sheltered valley site at Mád, and gave its name to the Holdvölgy winery, which works it along with neighbouring first-class sites.

sites.name: Juharos
sites.text: Juharos ('maple wood') is a Mád site in the official dűlő list, on volcanic tuff north of the village, producing fresh, mineral Furmint. Its northern position gives slow ripening, which suits dry styles more than aszú in most years.

sites.name: Kővágó
sites.text: Kővágó ('stone-cutter') is a stony Mád dűlő east of the village whose name recalls old quarrying; it makes firm, concentrated Furmint. Cut stone from the hill once went into Mád's houses and cellars, and the soil is correspondingly thin and rocky.

sites.name: Lapis
sites.text: Lapis (Latin for 'stone') is a terraced rhyolite slope above Bodrogkeresztúr. Királyudvar's Lapis Furmint and 6 Puttonyos Aszú made it famous, and the site produces taut, stony wines.

sites.name: Sajgó
sites.text: Sajgó lies on the Bodrogkeresztúr side of the Mád border, on volcanic tuff and clay, and gives powerful aszú berries. The site sits on the gentle saddle where the Mád valley opens toward the Bodrog, so river mist reaches it easily.

sites.name: Bendecz
sites.text: Bendecz is a Bodrogkeresztúr site south of the village center, on mixed volcanic soils, used for both dry and sweet wines by local growers. Like much of Bodrogkeresztúr, it benefits from the morning fogs rising off the river directly below.

sites.name: Kapi
sites.text: Kapi is a historic site on the Mezőzombor side of the Mád road, included in Disznókő's estate. In top botrytis years Disznókő bottles a single-vineyard Kapi 6 Puttonyos Aszú.

sites.name: Disznókő
sites.text: AXA Millésimes bought Disznókő ('boar's rock', first recorded 1413) in 1992 and rebuilt the winery beside the old press house. The estate is a single 150 ha block on a south-facing volcanic slope, planted with Furmint, Hárslevelű, Zéta and Sárgamuskotály. Its Aszú, Kapi single vineyard and '1413' sweet wine are benchmarks.

sites.name: Kassai
sites.text: Kassai (named after Košice) is a Tarcal site on Kassai-hegy, part loess and part volcanic. Kikelet's Stéphanie Berecz made it known for silky, aromatic dry Furmint and Hárslevelű from loess.

sites.name: Lónyai
sites.text: Lónyai, named after a noble family, is a loess-covered Tarcal slope whose dry Hárslevelű and Furmint from Kikelet are textbook loess wines: floral, round and fine.

sites.name: Váti
sites.text: Váti is a Tarcal site on the warm, loess-covered southern face of Tokaj hill, worked by Kikelet and others. The loess here is deep and fine, so the wines are perfumed, supple and approachable early, the opposite of Mád's flinty style.

sites.name: Mandulás
sites.text: Mandulás ('almond grove') is a Tarcal loess site on the warm southern side of Tokaj hill. Almond trees once grew between the vines, a sign of how sheltered and warm the slope is. The wines are soft and aromatic, typical of Tokaj hill's loess side.

sites.name: Előhegy
sites.text: Előhegy ('front hill') is a Tarcal hillside facing toward the Bodrog, on volcanic rock with loess patches. Its position on the hill's eastern flank catches the first morning sun and the Bodrog mists alike, a good combination for botrytis.

sites.name: Szentkereszt
sites.text: Szentkereszt ('holy cross') lies high on Tokaj hill above Tarcal, a mix of andesite and loess with long views over the Great Plain. It is one of the higher sites on Tokaj hill, so the wines combine loess softness with more lift and acidity.

sites.name: Hétszőlő
sites.text: Hétszőlő ('seven vineyards') was assembled from seven parcels by the Garai family in 1502 and later owned by Gáspár Károli, Gábor Bethlen, the Rákóczis and the Habsburgs. Its 55 ha of south-facing slopes on volcanic rock under loess now belong to Michel Reybier's Tokaj-Hétszőlő estate.

sites.name: Nagy-szőlő
sites.text: Nagy-szőlő ('big vineyard') is a loess site on the southern foot of Tokaj hill next to Hétszőlő. Its sheltered, low position by the Tisza floodplain makes it an early-ripening site with frequent botrytis.

sites.name: Teleki
sites.text: Teleki is a site on the southern foot of Tokaj hill near Hétszőlő, on loess-covered volcanic rock. It takes its name from the Teleki noble family, who held land in Tokaj, and shares the warm, loess-covered profile of its neighbour Hétszőlő.

sites.name: Padi-hegy
sites.text: Padi-hegy at Rátka is an andesite hill west of Mád whose slopes make structured, smoky Furmint. The hill's peak, Nagy-Padi, rises above the village, and its vineyards face south-east over the Mád valley.

sites.name: Hasznos
sites.text: Hasznos ('useful') is a Tállya site on andesite and volcanic tuff, known for firm, spicy wines. It lies on the hills north of the village toward Golop, a historically important part of the Rákóczi family's Tállya holdings.

sites.name: Kőporos (Ond)
sites.text: Kőporos ('stone dust') at Ond, now part of Szerencs, is a stony volcanic hillside whose name describes the powdery weathered rock underfoot. Ond's slopes face south over the Szerencs plain and were valued in the old classifications.

sites.name: Csirke-mál
sites.text: Csirke-mál ('chicken slope') in Bodrogkisfalud is a warm, sheltered south-facing site; 'mál' is an old word for a sunny hillside. Its warmth makes it a dependable source of ripe, botrytised fruit.

sites.name: Poklos
sites.text: Poklos is a Szegi site above the Bodrog, whose name hints at its hot ('hellish') sun exposure. The steep slope faces south over the river, so it gets both heat and the moisture that brings noble rot.

sites.name: Lőcse
sites.text: Lőcse, named after the Upper Hungarian town of Levoča, is a high Erdőbénye site of rhyolite tuff and loess where Béres makes fresh, mineral dry wines.

sites.name: Omlás
sites.text: Omlás ('landslide') is a steep Erdőbénye slope of weathered volcanic rock in the cool northern part of the region. Béres works it for dry Furmint with bright acidity, a reminder that the forested north of the region is markedly cooler than the south.

sites.name: Határi
sites.text: Határi ('border') sits on the line between Erdőbénye and Olaszliszka. Attila Homonna's dry Furmints from about 2005 drew attention to this forgotten, cool, stony slope.

sites.name: Csontos
sites.text: Csontos ('bony') is an Olaszliszka site whose name describes its stony, skeletal volcanic soil. Wines from such thin, rocky ground are typically tight and mineral, best after some years in bottle.

sites.name: Kincsem
sites.text: Kincsem ('my treasure') is a Tolcsva vineyard best known through Grand Tokaj and other Tolcsva producers; the name is shared with Hungary's legendary unbeaten racehorse.

sites.name: Petrács
sites.text: Petrács is a historic Tolcsva site belonging largely to Oremus, on volcanic soils above the village. The slope rises steeply behind Tolcsva and has long been prized for aszú berries.

sites.name: Kútpatka
sites.text: Kútpatka ('well's horseshoe') is a Tolcsva site whose fruit goes into Oremus's wines. It is a horseshoe-shaped hollow named for a well, and its sheltered bowl concentrates warmth.

sites.name: Pajzos
sites.text: The Pajzos vineyard lies in Bodrogolaszi just south of Sárospatak. Rated first class in 1772, its 107-ha estate was bought in 1991 by Jean-Louis Laborde's French group and is now the core of Pajzos-Megyer; its 1993 Esszencia earned a perfect score from the Wine Advocate.

sites.name: Megyer
sites.text: Megyer is a historic 110-ha vineyard on the hill above Végardó at Sárospatak. The French insurer GAN won it in the 1992 privatisation, and it was later merged with Pajzos. Its cooler northern position gives fresher, more aromatic wines.

sites.name: Oremus
sites.text: Oremus ('let us pray') is the vineyard on the castle hill of Sátoraljaújhely, owned by the Rákóczis. Legend makes it the source of Szepsi Laczkó Máté's first aszú (1631), and it was rated primae classis in 1772. Vega Sicilia's Tolcsva estate took its name.

sites.name: Royal Tokaji
sites.text: Founded in 1990 by Hugh Johnson, Danish winemaker Peter Vinding-Diers and about 60 Mád growers, Royal Tokaji was the first Western joint venture of the post-Communist era. It bought grapes until 1993 and now farms about 100 to 112 ha, including Mézes Mály, Szent Tamás, Betsek, Nyulászó and Birsalmás, which it labels with their historic first-growth ranks.

sites.name: Oremus (Tolcsva winery)
sites.text: The Álvarez family of Vega Sicilia founded Tokaj Oremus in 1993 at Tolcsva. The wines age in old tunnel cellars cut into the rock under the winery. Its dry Mandolás Furmint (since 2000) helped launch the dry wine revival, while its Aszú and Eszencia are among the most polished in the region.

sites.name: Pajzos-Megyer (Sárospatak)
sites.class: Winery, Sárospatak (formerly Château Pajzos and Château Megyer)
sites.text: The French investment group CFGVT, led by Jean-Louis Laborde, began buying in Tokaj in 1991; GAN won the Megyer vineyard in 1992. Laborde merged both into Pajzos Zrt around 2000. The Pajzos Esszencias of 1993 and 1999 both received 100 points from the Wine Advocate. The winery is on Nagy Lajos utca in Sárospatak.

sites.name: Szepsy
sites.text: István Szepsy, from a family of growers that traces its Tokaj roots to the 1500s, released his first Aszú in 1991 and, from the 2000 vintage, the dry single-vineyard Furmints (Szent Tamás, Úrágya, Betsek, Király and others) that redefined Tokaj. The family farms about 52 ha around Mád; his 6 Puttonyos 1999 is a Decanter 'wine legend'.

sites.name: Királyudvar
sites.text: Királyudvar ('royal court') occupies a historic royal court building in Tarcal. Anthony Hwang, owner of Domaine Huet in Vouvray, bought it in 1997; Zoltán Demeter and István Szepsy shaped its early wines. It farms biodynamically, and its Lapis vineyard Aszú and Cuvée Ilona late harvest are classics.

sites.name: Dobogó
sites.text: Dobogó is a small winery in the old town of Tokaj founded by Izabella Zwack, of the Unicum liqueur family, in the mid-1990s. It makes dry Furmint from Betsek, Aszú and the late-harvest Mylitta from first-class sites.

sites.name: Patricius
sites.text: Patricius was founded in 2000 by the Kékessy family in a restored 18th-century manor at Bodrogkisfalud. It owns about 85 ha in first-class sites and is known for dry Furmint, Katinka late harvest and long-aged Aszú.

sites.name: Grand Tokaj
sites.text: Grand Tokaj is the state-owned successor of the Communist-era Tokaj combine and the later Tokaj Kereskedőház, based at Tolcsva. It buys grapes from thousands of small growers and remains the region's largest producer, exporting to more than 30 countries. Its holdings include the great first growth Szarvas.

sites.name: Barta
sites.text: Károly Barta's family winery in Mád restored the abandoned, terraced Öreg Király ('old king') vineyard from 2003, one of the steepest slopes in Tokaj. The winery occupies an old Rákóczi-era mansion in the village.

sites.name: Samuel Tinon
sites.text: Samuel Tinon, from a Sainte-Croix-du-Mont winemaking family near Bordeaux, came to Tokaj in 1991 and settled at Olaszliszka. He is best known for reviving dry Szamorodni aged for years under a veil of yeast (flor), as well as long-macerated Aszú.

sites.name: Tokaj-Hétszőlő
sites.text: Tokaj-Hétszőlő owns 55 ha of the historic Hétszőlő vineyard on Tokaj hill. The French group GMF bought it in 1991; Michel Reybier, owner of Cos d'Estournel, has owned it since 2009. It is farmed organically and runs the Rákóczi cellar in Tokaj town for tastings.

sites.name: Holdvölgy
sites.text: Holdvölgy is a Mád estate founded in the 2000s with vineyards in Hold-völgy and neighbouring first-class sites. Its labyrinthine cellar under the village is used for tastings and ageing.

sites.name: Kikelet
sites.text: Kikelet ('springtime') is the small Tarcal estate of Stéphanie Berecz, who came from Bordeaux to work at Disznókő, and her husband Zsolt. Their dry Furmint and Hárslevelű from the loess sites Lónyai, Váti and Kassai showed how fine loess wines can be.

sites.name: Béres
sites.text: Béres farms about 45 ha in the cool northern sites around Erdőbénye, including Lőcse, Diókút and Omlás. Its winery sits among the vines above the village.

sites.name: Rákóczi Cellar, Sárospatak
sites.text: Beneath the Rákóczi castle in Sárospatak runs a cellar labyrinth of several branches cut into volcanic tuff, used by the princes to store the wine of their Hegyalja estates. Their Tokaji served as a diplomatic gift, notably to Louis XIV. The castle and cellar are now a museum and tasting venue.

sites.name: Rákóczi Castle, Sárospatak
sites.text: The Renaissance castle on the Bodrog was the seat of the Rákóczi princes, owners of great Tokaj vineyards. Zsuzsanna Lorántffy lived here, and Ferenc II Rákóczi led the 1703 to 1711 war of independence from these lands, using Tokaji as diplomatic currency.

sites.name: Rákóczi Cellar, Tokaj
sites.text: This cellar under Tokaj's main square, beside the church, dates from the early 15th century. Its knights' hall (28 m long, 10 m wide, 5 m high) is said to be the largest underground hall in the region. Its walls are coated with black cellar mould, and it is used today for tastings.

sites.name: Tokaj Museum
sites.text: The Tokaj Museum occupies an 18th-century Greek merchant's house in Tokaj town. Greek traders were key middlemen in the 18th-century Tokaji trade. Its exhibits cover the history of Tokaji wine, coopering and the town's Greek, Jewish and Hungarian communities.

sites.name: Kőporos cellar row, Hercegkút
sites.text: Two streets of cellars dug into the hill above Hercegkút (Kőporos and Gombos-hegy), most with small stone or plastered fronts, form part of the core zone of the UNESCO Tokaj landscape. They show the small-grower cellar culture of the German-speaking settlers.

sites.name: Szepsi Laczkó Máté Memorial House
sites.text: In Erdőbénye a small memorial house honours Máté Szepsi Laczkó (c. 1576 to 1632/33), the Reformed pastor credited by legend with the first aszú. Historians doubt the claim, since his own chronicle never mentions aszú, but the story remains central to Tokaj's identity.

sites.name: Mád Synagogue
sites.text: This late-18th-century baroque synagogue in Mád, restored in the 2000s, recalls the Jewish families who dominated the Tokaji trade, produced kosher wine for Polish and Russian markets and owned many cellars until the Holocaust.

sites.name: Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape (UNESCO)
sites.text: UNESCO inscribed the Tokaj landscape in 2002, with a core area of 13,255 ha and a buffer of 74,879 ha. It recognises a living tradition of viticulture and winemaking, with its pattern of vineyards, villages and rock-cut cellars. The point marks the summit of Tokaj hill (Kopasz-hegy, 514 m).

sites.name: Eger Castle
sites.text: In 1552 István Dobó's garrison of about 2,000 held Eger castle for 39 days against a far larger Ottoman army. Later legend says red wine stained the defenders' beards and the Turks thought they drank bull's blood, the story behind Egri Bikavér. Eger fell in 1596 and stayed Ottoman until 1687.

sites.name: Szépasszony-völgy
sites.text: The 'Valley of the Beautiful Woman' on the south-west edge of Eger is lined with around 200 cellars cut into soft rhyolite tuff, many now tasting rooms. It is the classic place to taste Egri Bikavér from the barrel, and the name's origin (a pagan goddess, a beautiful innkeeper) is still argued over.

sites.name: Nagy-Eged
sites.text: Nagy-Eged is the steep limestone and tuff hill north-east of Eger, rising to about 535 m, with south-facing terraces. It is considered the town's finest red-wine site, especially for Kékfrankos and Pinot Noir, and features in many Grand Superior Bikavérs.

sites.name: Villány cellar row and Wine Museum
sites.text: Villány's Baross Gábor and Batthyány streets are lined with the cellars and press houses of the German-descended families who rebuilt the area after the Ottoman wars. The Wine Museum occupies an 18th-century cellar in the middle of the row.

sites.name: Palkonya cellar village
sites.text: Palkonya's whitewashed press houses, about 50 of them, run in a row along a single lane below the vines. The village, settled by Swabians, is one of the best-preserved small cellar villages in the Villány district.

sites.name: Kopár
sites.text: Kopár ('bare') is a steep, stony south-facing limestone slope at Nagyharsány. Its name describes how thin the topsoil is. Gere Attila's flagship red, a Cabernet Franc-led blend, is named after it, and it remains Villány's best-known single vineyard.

sites.name: Jammertal
sites.text: Jammertal ('valley of lamentation') is a historic Villány vineyard. Its name is said to recall a battle near here in the 1687 campaign. It is now planted with Cabernet Franc and other reds and is home to the Jammertal hotel and winery.

sites.name: Heimann & Fiai
sites.text: The Heimann family estate in the Iván valley near Szekszárd has led the revival of Kadarka, collecting and replanting old local clones. It also makes some of the district's finest Bikavér and Cabernet Franc.

sites.name: Somló hill
sites.text: A lone extinct volcano rising to 432 m out of the flat Kisalföld, Somló is topped by a castle ruin and wrapped in small vineyards and press houses. Its basalt soils give Hungary's most mineral whites, the Juhfark-led 'wedding night wine' said to guarantee a son.

sites.name: Badacsony hill
sites.text: Badacsony is a coffin-shaped basalt butte on the north shore of Lake Balaton. Its columnar basalt 'organ pipes' tower over terraces of Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát and Kéknyelű, and poet Sándor Kisfaludy's press house still stands on its slope.

sites.name: Szent György-hegy
sites.text: Szent György-hegy (415 m) near Tapolca is a basalt witness hill whose columnar 'organ pipes' and old press houses make it one of the most beautiful vineyard hills in Hungary. Its wines are part of the Badacsony PDO.

sites.name: Tihany Benedictine Abbey
sites.text: Founded in 1055 by King Andrew I, the abbey on the Tihany peninsula owned vineyards from its first charter. That charter is famous for containing the oldest surviving written Hungarian words. The peninsula is now a red-wine PDO.

sites.name: Pannonhalma Archabbey Winery
sites.text: The Benedictine archabbey founded in 996, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996, has grown wine for a millennium. Its modern winery, rebuilt in 2003 on the old vineyard terraces, makes Rajnai rizling, Sauvignon Blanc, Tramini and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Törley, Budafok
sites.text: József Törley learned sparkling winemaking in Reims and in 1882 moved his business to Budafok on the southern edge of Budapest, attracted by its limestone cellars and nearby vineyards. Törley remains Hungary's biggest sparkling wine house; the family's mansion is nearby.

sites.name: Hajós cellar village
sites.text: Outside the village of Hajós lies a separate 'village' of more than 1,200 cellars and press houses in neat streets, built by Swabian settlers from the 18th century. It is one of the largest cellar villages in Central Europe and hosts a festival every May.

sites.name: Fertőrákos quarry
sites.text: This Leitha limestone quarry beside Lake Fertő has been worked since Roman times. Stone from here helped build Vienna, and its huge cavern halls are part of the Fertő/Neusiedlersee UNESCO landscape. The same limestone underlies some of Sopron's Kékfrankos vineyards.

sites.name: Kecskemét and the sand vineyards
sites.text: Kecskemét is the hub of the Kunság. In 1883 the town gave the state land for the Miklóstelep demonstration vineyard, which proved that vines on loose sand escape phylloxera. Commissioner Gyula Miklós's experiment made the Great Plain Hungary's largest vineyard.

sites.name: Aldebrő and Feldebrő
sites.text: The twin villages of Aldebrő and Feldebrő at the eastern foot of the Mátra are the heart of the Debrői Hárslevelű PDO. Feldebrő's church has a crypt with 11th-century frescoes, among the oldest in Hungary.

sites.name: Csopak
sites.text: Csopak lies on the north-east shore of Lake Balaton among slopes of red Permian sandstone and slate. Its growers' 2012 'Csopak Codex' and the 2020 Csopak PDO made Olaszrizling a serious terroir wine.

sites.name: Kőszeg
sites.text: Kőszeg is a walled town on the Austrian border with its own PDO since 2025. Every year since 1740 the town has drawn the length of the young vine shoots on St George's Day into its 'Book of the Coming of the Grapes', a rare record of budbreak.
